subject: Agriculture
title: Flood Irrigation
description: A fast breakdown of Flood Irrigation for builders.

hook.text: Flood irrigation is the oldest method still in wide use. Water flows across the field by gravity.

buildup.text: Farmers open a gate, and water spreads across leveled basins or runs down furrows between crop rows.

discovery.text: It's cheap—no pumps, no pipes, just gravity and a flat field. That's why 85% of irrigated land uses it.

twist.text: Flood irrigation wastes up to 50% of the water applied. Much evaporates, runs off, or seeps too deep.

climax.text: As water scarcity grows, regions are slowly shifting away—but replacing flood systems costs billions.

punchline.text: The cheapest irrigation is also the most wasteful.

quiz.question: What is the main drawback of flood irrigation?
options: It wastes up to 50% of applied water through evaporation and runoff
It only works on flat land

details.summary: Flood irrigation is the oldest and simplest method—covering fields with a layer of water and letting it soak in. This topic covers how flood irrigation works, why it still dominates globally despite low efficiency, and the prospects for improvement.
details.whyItMatters: Flood irrigation still waters over 80% of the world's irrigated land yet wastes 40–60% of applied water. Improving flood practices or transitioning to efficient methods could free enormous water resources.
takeaways: Flood irrigation applies water across entire fields, allowing gravity to distribute it
It remains dominant because of low cost and minimal infrastructure requirements
Laser-leveling fields can improve flood irrigation efficiency by 25% or more

faq.question: How does flood irrigation work?
faq.answer: Water is released from canals or pumps and flows over the entire field surface, filling furrows or basins. Gravity distributes the water, which soaks into the soil. Plants absorb what they need while the rest evaporates, runs off, or percolates deep.

faq.question: Why is flood irrigation considered inefficient?
faq.answer: Flood irrigation loses 40–60% of applied water to evaporation, runoff, and deep percolation below the root zone. It applies water uniformly regardless of varying soil or crop needs, over-irrigating some areas while under-irrigating others.
